title: Flood damage at your Vero Beach home? How to report it to the county, and where to ask for help
seoTitle: Vero Beach Flood Damage: How to Report It to the County
description: Indian River County is asking Vero Beach homeowners to report damage from this week's flooding. Where the online form is, what it asks, and who else can help.
dek: County damage teams started surveying neighborhoods on Thursday, and the county wants to hear from you too. Reporting takes a few minutes online. Here is what the form asks, why your report counts, and the other places to turn this week.
facebook: Did this week's flood leave its mark on your Vero Beach home? Indian River County is asking homeowners to report the damage online, and it only takes a few minutes. Here's where the form is, what it asks, and who else can help right now.

body.text: Monday's rain was not normal rain. Vero Beach Regional Airport recorded 4.91 inches on Nov. 2, breaking the old record for that day of 2.63 inches, set in 2009. The National Weather Service said it was at least a 500- to 1,000-year rainfall event. Preliminary weather service reports show 13 to 16 inches across the county over the storm.

Now the water is going down, and the county wants to know what it left behind. Indian River County is asking residents and business owners to report property damage from the rain and flooding. Damage assessment teams began surveying residential areas on Thursday, Nov. 5.

body.title: The short version
body.text: If flooding damaged your home, report it on the county's online form: crisistrack.juvare.com/public/indianriverFL/request.html. Have your address, a short description of the damage and your contact information ready. Add photos only if it is safe to take them.
What the county is asking for

Ryan Lloyd is deputy director and chief of emergency management for Indian River County. He told WQCS: "We are asking residents and businesses to use the link provided to assist us in documenting the impacts of this event."
The form is short. According to WQCS, it asks for three things:

items: The address of the damaged property.

body.text: You can upload photos with your report. The county says to do that only when it is safe. Do not wade into standing water or walk into a room with wet wiring just to get a picture.
Why one report from your street matters

The county says the reports help it document what this storm did and figure out what people need to recover. Think of it as a head count for damage. A few reports from one neighborhood look like a small problem. Dozens of reports from the same streets show where help is needed most.

Damage counts also matter beyond the county line. Under federal rules, a preliminary damage assessment is how local, state and federal teams measure the size of a disaster and the needs it left behind. The state uses those results to support a governor's request for federal help. That does not mean federal aid is coming for this flood. No source has said that. It means the paperwork that could lead there starts with counts like this one.
One more thing to know: nothing the county has shared about the form says that filing a report signs you up for any aid program. It is a way to tell the county what happened at your address.
Other places to turn this week
CBS12 put together a list of resources for Indian River County residents on Thursday. Here are the ones that apply to homeowners:

items: United Way of Indian River County is taking disaster assistance requests through an online form listed in CBS12's resource roundup.
The American Red Cross has an online tool at redcross.org to find open shelters if you cannot stay in your home.
Indian River County's emergency management office keeps a page on disaster grants, loans and insurance information at indianriver.gov.

If you also own a business, the state is collecting damage reports at FloridaDisaster.biz. Pick "2026 Fall Flooding" from the list. The survey covers 14 counties, including Indian River. The state's private sector hotline is 850-815-4925, open daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

body.text: A plain fact worth knowing as you sort things out: the county's own flood information notes that flood losses are typically not covered under most homeowners policies. If you are not sure what your policy covers, your insurance agent can explain it.

items: Walk your house in daylight once the water is gone. Check floors, the bottom of walls, cabinets, the garage, and any outside A/C or pool equipment.
Take dated photos from a safe spot. Wide shots first, then close-ups. Keep them in one folder on your phone.
Write down what you saw and when: how high the water got, how long it sat, and which rooms it reached.
File the county report online with your address, a short description and your contact information.
Tell your neighbors. If water came into three houses on your street, the county should hear about all three.
If you need help now, such as a place to stay or basic supplies, use the United Way form or the Red Cross shelter tool.
Keep avoiding flooded roads and obey every barricade. The county repeated that warning this week.

body.text: The beach took a hit too. Parts of the Conn Beach boardwalk were closed after erosion from the storm. If you head to the ocean this weekend, respect the closed sections.
For general county questions, Indian River County's main number is 772-567-8000. The county administration building is at 1801 27th Street in Vero Beach.

faq.q: How do I report flood damage in Indian River County?
faq.a: Use the county's online damage reporting form at crisistrack.juvare.com/public/indianriverFL/request.html. It asks for the property address, a description of the damage and your contact information. You can add photos if it is safe to take them.

faq.q: Is Indian River County doing damage assessments after the November 2026 flooding?
faq.a: Yes. WQCS reported that county damage assessment teams began surveying residential areas on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, to document impacts and identify recovery needs.

faq.q: Does reporting damage to the county mean I will get disaster aid?
faq.a: Not by itself. The county says the reports help it document the storm's impact and identify recovery needs. No source has said federal aid has been approved for this flood.

faq.q: How much rain fell in Vero Beach on Nov. 2, 2026?
faq.a: Vero Beach Regional Airport recorded 4.91 inches on Nov. 2, 2026, breaking the daily record of 2.63 inches set in 2009. Preliminary National Weather Service reports show 13 to 16 inches across the county over the storm.

faq.q: Where can I get help after the flood in Indian River County?
faq.a: United Way of Indian River County is taking disaster assistance requests through an online form, and the American Red Cross has an online shelter finder at redcross.org. The county's emergency management office lists disaster grants, loans and insurance information at indianriver.gov.
